chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Said from Hammad ibn Isa al-Juhani from Umar ibn Udhaynah from more than one from Abu Ja'far and Abu Abdillah (peace be upon them both)

That they were asked about a man who has a house, a servant, and a slave who accepts alms-tax, so they said: 'Yes, indeed the house and the servant are not considered property (wealth subject to khums/zakat limits).'
ai.seo_question: Can a person with a house and servants receive zakat?
ai.summary: This hadith from the Tahdhib clarifies the Shia jurisprudential distinction between essential living assets and disposable wealth, establishing that a house, servant, and slave are considered functional necessities rather than liquid capital (mal) that disqualifies one from zakat. This ruling reflects the practical reality of pre-modern society where such assets were integral to maintaining one's social standing and livelihood, rather than mere stores of value. It underscores the Shia emphasis on the recipient's actual capacity for self-sufficiency rather than a rigid inventory of all possessions.
